name: Charles Howard
bio: Charles Howard was president of the Baltimore Board of Police Commissioners. On July 1, 1861, after federal authorities seized control of the city's police, he and his fellow commissioners were arrested by Union troops and imprisoned without trial or charge — first at Fort McHenry, then at Fort Lafayette in New York Harbor, and later at Fort Warren in Boston. They were held for more than a year before being released.
charges: Arrested and held without trial as part of the federal suppression of Confederate-sympathizing officials in Baltimore, after the U.S. Army seized control of the city police.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry, then Fort Lafayette and Fort Warren, for more than a year.

name: Severn Teackle Wallis
bio: Severn Teackle Wallis was a distinguished Baltimore lawyer and man of letters and a member of the Maryland House of Delegates. He was among the roughly thirty state legislators and officials seized in the September 1861 federal arrests meant to prevent a feared secession vote, and was imprisoned without charge at Fort McHenry and then Fort Warren for some fourteen months.
charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge to forestall any secession vote.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Imprisoned about fourteen months at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

name: Lawrence Sangston
bio: Lawrence Sangston was a member of the Maryland House of Delegates arrested in the September 1861 federal seizure of the legislature and held without charge at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren. He later published an account of his imprisonment, 'The Bastiles of the North' (1863).
charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

bio: Henry M. Warfield was a member of the Maryland House of Delegates arrested in the September 1861 federal sweep of the legislature and imprisoned without charge at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.
charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.

sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

name: Harkins Scott
bio: Harkins Scott was a Maryland legislator arrested in the September 1861 federal sweep of the state legislature and held without charge at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.
charges: Arrested in the September 1861 sweep of the Maryland legislature and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry and Fort Warren.

name: George Armistead Appleton
bio: George Armistead Appleton was a Baltimore civilian detained without charge during the federal suppression of secessionist activity in Maryland and held at Fort McHenry.
charges: Detained without charge during the federal crackdown on Confederate sympathizers in Baltimore.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry.

name: Robert Douglas
bio: The Reverend Robert Douglas was a Baltimore-area clergyman detained during the federal crackdown on Confederate sympathizers in Maryland and listed among the political prisoners held at Fort McHenry.
charges: Detained without charge during the federal suppression of secessionist sympathy in Maryland.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner.
sentence: Held at Fort McHenry.

name: Richard Bennett Carmichael
bio: Richard Bennett Carmichael was a Maryland circuit-court judge who, from the bench, denounced the arbitrary arrests of citizens for disloyalty. In May 1862 federal officers dragged him from his own courtroom while court was in session, beating and arresting him, and held him without charge for more than five months at Fort McHenry, Fort Lafayette, and Fort Delaware.
charges: Arrested from the bench in May 1862 after criticizing arbitrary arrests, and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held more than five months at Fort McHenry, Fort Lafayette, and Fort Delaware.

name: James W. Wall
bio: James W. Wall was a New Jersey Democratic politician and newspaper editor arrested in September 1861 for his antiwar and anti-administration writings and held without charge at Fort Lafayette for about two weeks. He was later elected to the U.S. Senate from New Jersey in 1863.
charges: Arrested for antiwar, anti-administration journalism and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held about two weeks at Fort Lafayette.

name: Pierce Butler
bio: Pierce Butler was a wealthy Philadelphia landowner and grandson of the Founding Father of the same name — infamous for the 1859 'Weeping Time,' the largest single sale of enslaved people in U.S. history. A Southern sympathizer, he was arrested in August 1861 and held without charge at Fort Lafayette for about a month.
charges: Arrested as a suspected Confederate sympathizer and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held about a month at Fort Lafayette.

name: James G. Berrett
bio: James G. Berrett was the mayor of Washington, D.C., arrested in August 1861 after he refused to take a federal loyalty oath. He was imprisoned without charge at Fort Lafayette and resigned the mayoralty as a condition of his release.
charges: Arrested for refusing a loyalty oath and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner; released after resigning as mayor.
sentence: Held at Fort Lafayette.

name: Charles James Faulkner
bio: Charles James Faulkner was a former U.S. congressman from Virginia and U.S. minister to France. On returning from his diplomatic post in 1861 he was arrested and held without charge at Fort Warren, then exchanged in December 1861 for the captured Union congressman Alfred Ely. He later served the Confederacy.
charges: Arrested on returning from his post as U.S. minister to France and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner; exchanged.
sentence: Held at Fort Warren, then exchanged in December 1861.

name: Charles S. Morehead
bio: Charles S. Morehead was a former governor of Kentucky (1855–1859). Suspected of Confederate sympathies, he was arrested in September 1861 and imprisoned without charge at Fort Lafayette and Fort Warren before being released in 1862.
charges: Arrested as a suspected Confederate sympathizer and held without charge.
convicted: No — held without trial as a political prisoner and released.
sentence: Held at Fort Lafayette and Fort Warren.

name: George Eustis Jr.
bio: George Eustis Jr. was secretary to the Confederate diplomatic mission of James M. Mason and John Slidell. He was seized with them aboard the British steamer Trent on November 8, 1861 — the Trent Affair that nearly brought Britain into the war — and held at Fort Warren until the commissioners were released in January 1862.
charges: Seized in the Trent Affair as secretary to the Confederate diplomatic mission and held without charge.
convicted: No — held as a political prisoner; released to defuse the Trent Affair.
sentence: Held at Fort Warren, November 1861 – January 1862.

name: John H. Reagan
bio: John H. Reagan was the Confederate Postmaster General. Captured with Jefferson Davis's fleeing party in Georgia in May 1865, he was imprisoned as a state prisoner at Fort Warren for some months. He later returned to public life as a U.S. congressman and senator from Texas.
charges: Captured with the Confederate government's fleeing party in May 1865 and held as a state prisoner.
convicted: No — held without trial and released.
sentence: Held at Fort Warren for several months in 1865.

name: Edward A. Pollard
bio: Edward A. Pollard was the editor of the Richmond Examiner and a prominent Confederate journalist, later author of 'The Lost Cause.' Captured in 1864 while attempting to run the blockade to Europe, he was held as a prisoner at Fort Warren and Fortress Monroe before being exchanged.
charges: Captured running the blockade and held as a Confederate political prisoner.
convicted: No — held as a political prisoner; exchanged.
sentence: Held at Fort Warren and Fortress Monroe.

name: Jefferson Davis
bio: Jefferson Davis was the president of the Confederate States of America. Captured in Georgia on May 10, 1865, he was held as a state prisoner at Fortress Monroe in Virginia — for a time in shackles — and indicted for treason. He was never tried; released on bail in May 1867, and the charges were dropped in 1869.
charges: Captured at the end of the Civil War and held as a state prisoner, indicted for treason but never tried.
convicted: No — indicted for treason but never brought to trial; released on bail and the charge later dropped.
sentence: Held about two years at Fortress Monroe, 1865–1867; released on bail May 13, 1867.

name: William A. Bowles
bio: William A. Bowles was an Indiana physician and a leader of the Sons of Liberty, an antiwar secret society. Arrested in 1864, he was tried before a military commission at Indianapolis alongside Lambdin P. Milligan and sentenced to death. He was freed after the Supreme Court's 1866 decision in Ex parte Milligan held that civilians could not be tried by military tribunals where the civil courts were open.
charges: Tried by a military commission at Indianapolis as an antiwar Sons of Liberty conspirator.
convicted: Yes — convicted by military commission and sentenced to death; freed after Ex parte Milligan (1866).
sentence: Sentenced to death; released in 1866 following the Supreme Court's ruling in Ex parte Milligan.

name: Stephen Horsey
bio: Stephen Horsey was an Indiana antiwar Democrat tried before a military commission at Indianapolis with Lambdin P. Milligan and William A. Bowles and sentenced to death. He was freed in 1866 after the Supreme Court's decision in Ex parte Milligan.
charges: Tried by a military commission at Indianapolis as an antiwar conspirator.
convicted: Yes — convicted by military commission and sentenced to death; freed after Ex parte Milligan (1866).
sentence: Sentenced to death; released in 1866 following Ex parte Milligan.

name: Andrew Humphreys
bio: Andrew Humphreys was an Indiana antiwar Democrat tried before a military commission at Indianapolis in the Sons of Liberty case connected to Lambdin P. Milligan. Convicted, he was sentenced to hard labor for the duration of the war, and his case was among those resolved by the Supreme Court's 1866 ruling in Ex parte Milligan.
charges: Tried by a military commission at Indianapolis as an antiwar conspirator.
convicted: Yes — convicted by military commission; sentence commuted, then voided under Ex parte Milligan (1866).
sentence: Sentenced to hard labor; freed following Ex parte Milligan.

name: Harrison H. Dodd
bio: Harrison H. Dodd was the Grand Commander of the Sons of Liberty in Indiana. Arrested in 1864 and tried by a military commission at Indianapolis for an alleged antiwar conspiracy, he escaped from custody before his verdict and fled; he was convicted in absentia.
charges: Tried by a military commission at Indianapolis as the leader of the Sons of Liberty antiwar conspiracy.
convicted: Yes — convicted in absentia by military commission after escaping custody.
sentence: Escaped custody before sentencing; convicted in absentia.

name: Benjamin Gwinn Harris
bio: Benjamin Gwinn Harris was a Maryland congressman and outspoken opponent of the war. In 1865 he was convicted by a military commission for allegedly aiding and harboring Confederate soldiers and sentenced to imprisonment and disqualification from office; the imprisonment was remitted by President Andrew Johnson.
charges: Convicted by a military commission for allegedly aiding and harboring Confederate soldiers.
convicted: Yes — convicted by military commission; imprisonment remitted by President Johnson.
sentence: Sentenced to imprisonment and permanent disqualification from office; the prison term was remitted.
